quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6, The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986 (trans. Patrick Creagh)

evidence.where: The New York Review of Books text of Why Read the Classics? was read: the sentence stands as the numbered definition 6, between definition 5 on every reading of a classic being a rereading and definition 7 on the traces of previous readings, and the article credits the translation to Patrick Creagh. The later Martin McLaughlin translation renders the same definition as a book which has never exhausted all it has to say to its readers, so the wording proposed is Creagh's and the source must name him.
evidence.edition: The New York Review of Books, 9 October 1986, trans. Patrick Creagh, English translation copyright Harcourt Brace Jovanovich

reason: The wording, the number of the definition and the translator all hold in the 1986 Creagh translation, which is the one this wording comes from.
